I love all the games made by this developer so far: [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1603410/Lost_Nova/?utm_source=MissiTheAchievementHuntress&utm_campaign=steam_achievement_hunting&utm_medium=world_wide_webby&utm_content=confabulate_reviews&utm_term=having_fun&curator_clanid=33025671/]Lost Nova[/url], [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1842510/Mechanibot/?utm_source=MissiTheAchievementHuntress&utm_campaign=steam_achievement_hunting&utm_medium=world_wide_webby&utm_content=confabulate_reviews&utm_term=having_fun&curator_clanid=33025671/]Mechanibot[/url], and I'm so glad he didn't break that streak (yet, and hopefully never will)! This game is a lot like Stacklands, where you stack cards to combine them into something new. But in this game, the theme is witches and magic. The developer did such an awesome job with the artwork, it looks magical. The style fits the theme so well and I'm glad he went for the magical theme. Before I started playing this I was a bit scared. Am I smart enough and organized enough to play a game that has more in it than Stacklands has? And I can say that sometimes my playing field was a mess, but nothing I couldn't clean up. So yeah I'm smart enough and organized enough to be able to play this, as it has spells later on to help you organize things, and the game isn't hard to understand or to master (until that last encounter, that one is a challenge for sure). The achievements are what makes sense in a game like this. some might be a bit grindy but before you reach the ending you'll have unlocked most of them and some others have become so much easier to grind out. The scariest thing is that when you die in a run, you lose your progress and have to start all over again. if you lost by mere seconds, it is worth it to not start a new run but to choose "quit" when the pop-up comes up and go back to your save files. However, I would highly recommend just backup your save file regularly while playing through WitchHand so you don't lose too much if you die.

Honestly just too much going on, which is surprising, and some people might be into that. But I certainly wouldn't call it relaxing. It's like a standard colony builder, except you have to micromanage every single character in your colony for every action they perform - and you even have to micromanage every single resource your colony produces, moving them to the next thing in the production chain or just to a random storage pile in the corner I think the fundamental problem is that even if you don't upgrade anything or build anything to increase the cap, by default, you have a cap of 3 summons plus yourself (and can easily summon them all). Which means the general gameplay at the start is playing Cultist Simulator 4 times at once on the same board, pausing each time any of your four characters do anything, and trying desperately to find things for all four of them to do. And then you build an upgrade and now there's 6 characters to handle, and that upgrade is cheap and repeatable Obviously you don't have to be efficient, you can just leave them sitting around doing nothing, but then why are they even there Plus, you've got a board with a limited size (for some reason), just filled with random piles of resources that keep getting bumped around because there's no room for production to place new ones, so it moves existing ones. And of course, there's no snapping to keep them organized, so it all just ends up a giant mess that you could never feasibly clean up All that aside, it's clean and feels good and is well polished and seems to have lots of content - it's a well made game. But the basic concept of the game seems doomed to fail

Being beholden to timers and RNG, particularly with regards to resource management/distribution, left me falling at the same hurdle on 6 out of 7 runs, seemingly without the means to actually overcome said hurdle (or those means being provided too late to be meaningful/useful). There is the framework for a good game underneath this, particularly if you have played something like sokpop's Stacklands before, but not being able to retain/gain the materials you need to make any meaningful progress robs the experience of any joy.

EDIT: beat the first boss, not going to bother going for the second given how much busywork is involved. I'm not going to refund, and I am going to see it through. But this game is simply frustrating to play at all levels. With no snapping, long, long strings of resources butting into each other as part of regular gameplay, and a lot of tedious repetition (as an example; to grow silversage you consume one to get two back, meaning that it's a bottleneck early until you RNG into it and harvesting the process can't be automated with Magnets), this game learnt the wrong lessons from Stacklands. 90% of the gameplay is just sorting cards into where they should go since the automation options are either not useful or not available until several hours in. And when you fail a run you fail hard, you have a choice of either going back a few seconds before your death or restarting; there are no save states. I can see how some people would enjoy this but the sheer number of positive reviews this game is getting confuses me. Avoid.

Legally, I'm sure they can do this, but morally, it crosses a line. Go play Stacklands, the game that this game is ripping off.

I really, REALLY wanted to like this game, it's got a lot going for it. At the end of the day there's just too much false progress and gating for me to really recommend it. False Progress : Your primary repeated action is exploring, on a card which costs (at least) 3 gp to buy. As part of the exploration, you always get a mine as one of the rewards, which, surprise, peters out after giving you 3gp. So, instead of 'exploring' being a free action that takes 10 seconds, it instead takes 5 seconds, +5 seconds on a secondary task to get your money back. False progress and busy work to make the grind 'feel' better. Gating: There's a ton of interesting cards flying around and rewards, and stuff to do, but it takes all of 5 minutes into the game to realize it's all window dressing on the daily reward(in game day) which gates your progress. Everything else is just making sure you're earning at least enough resources during that day to be able to take advantage of your new space. The game feels deep, after 6 hours, I was still encountering new stuff pretty regularly, but with the gating, it's really just a cat herding game while you wait until the next day. Some other complaints: The difficulty is weird. You get 4 hit points (at least with the character I was playing), and get hit by any monsters still alive at the end of the day, but there's no guarantee you won't get hit (or even killed), by monsters that spawn too late for you to do anything about. (This might just be the slimes, which spawn new enemies when killed, spawning too late in the day, but considering the rogue-like death penalty, it feels harsh for a grinding game like this) There also needs to be a serious QoL pass over the functionality, especially around cards popping, displacement, and chests. Items shouldn't push their chest out of the way when they pop on them, and the default chest auto-collect range should be MUCH higher for the amount of cards popping. All this comes from a place of love, for the game, and the genre. It needs some polish and balancing, and I'm hoping when I come back later this year, it'll all be better, because the core is worth the effort.

I believe games like Stacklands, which I first experienced and thoroughly enjoyed, could mark the rise of a new genre I'd like to call "Card Factory" games. These games create a unique sensation of managing a card-based production system, a concept I'm eager to see evolve. WitchHand takes this idea further by incorporating a charming magical theme. I was so captivated by it that I unlocked every achievement available. Despite my overall enjoyment, I encountered some frustrations, such as the ineffective "lock card" feature, which failed to keep cards stationary. Additionally, the spawning of traders and other events often disrupted my setup by appearing in the middle of my buildings and displacing them. Aside from the annoyance of cards moving unexpectedly and cluttering the play area, I genuinely appreciated the game and am excited about the potential growth of this genre.

This is an addicting 4x game with card stacking mechanics, but issues with progression and a lack of an ending mean I don't recommend this game. The game revolves around stacking cards to do actions and craft more cards. As you continue to stack more cards, more types of cards are revealed. This cards let you make cities, fight enemies, cast spells, etc. which is a neat take on abstracting the 4x genre. The art and music are also very nice. They have a cute witchy feel to them I haven't seen for 4Xs either. Progress is a bit too slow, but fairly steady for most of the game. The main issues I have to do with progression. Like many 4Xs the late game is a slog(though admittedly it is still challenging). The game feels like it ends once before the actual end game and it had no indication of it so I had to look through the discussions to confirm I had even hit an ending. I also frequently ran into space issues in the mid game because of how the map is expanded and performance issues in the late game because my production chains and the spoils of combat where causing hundreds of cards to spawn, move, and collide. I had fun with the game, and I don't regret buying it on a discount, but I don't think I'll be recommending it to others.

The game is OK, I would give a mixed review if I could. I played about 3 hours, and the game just seems very bland. You just spend 90% of your time split between creating cards and putting your workers to either explore or generate some resource. When a resource gets generated, the card flails around and you have to position them where you want. There are no big decisions to make, when an enemy appears, you kill it. If there's an "explore" card, you explore it. If there's a building that you don't have, then make it. There are no ways of doing something wrong, no big objective, just positive feedback loops. I feel like I'm making cards just because. There's also some needed QoL features, because I feel like most of my time playing this is spent making sure that my board doesn't look like a mess. Is it really needed to generate so many cards? Even with using the chest, things are only put there if it's generated nearby. If you're into this type of game, no punishment, just creating stuff, then you're probably going to like it. I prefer playing Cultist Simulator over this.
